evaluation.positioning_hook: A retired Vegas cage fighter with a brain cyst and a sick daughter is forced back into underground bouts by a criminal promoter who owns his life, his home, and the clock on his child’s survival.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The emotional engine is instantly legible: a father fighting to save his daughter, with brutal fight scenes and a clear villain. The audience is narrower than a four-quadrant action title because the material is hard-edged and heavily male-skewing, but the hook is strong and commercial.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands immediately in the opening fight, then sharpens with the cyst reveal, the daughter’s illness, and Cisco’s leverage. The script keeps the central question clean: how long can Billy keep fighting before his body, his conscience, or Cisco breaks him first?

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Billy has a durable contradiction: a violent man who is also a tender, exhausted dad, and that gives the role range. Rollie, Jasmine, Claudia, and Cisco all have clear functions and texture, though Billy remains the only truly deep engine.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script leans into a specific, bruised world of swamp fights, casino backrooms, and medical desperation rather than generic sports-drama terrain. The boldest move is making the hero’s body both his weapon and his death sentence.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story is built on escalating pressure: fight money, medical bills, Cisco’s manipulation, Claudia’s worsening condition, and the final kidnapping. The second half in particular keeps tightening the vise with repeated fight/payoff cycles that feel purpose-built for momentum.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The core idea is simple and sticky: a damaged fighter can only save his daughter by risking the one thing that will kill him. It’s familiar in shape, but the cyst, the swamp-fight ecosystem, and the father-daughter medical stakes give it a fresh commercial angle.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The script builds a vivid underworld with Vegas backrooms, Shreveport riverboat casinos, swamp fights, crooked doctors, and a fight promoter who doubles as a criminal operator. The setting feels story-generating rather than decorative, with money, violence, and leverage all embedded in the world.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is consistently bruising, sentimental, and muscular, with occasional humor from Jimmy and the domestic scenes with Claudia. It’s recognizable and playable, though it sits closer to a strong genre-drama register than a truly singular tonal signature.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are deeper layers around masculinity, bodily decline, fatherhood, and the ethics of violence, but the script largely states those themes through plot rather than subtext. The emotional material is real, yet the page is more immediate than layered.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Billy/Rollie, Billy/Jasmine, Billy/Claudia, and Billy/Cisco each generate distinct energy, and the supporting cast is functional rather than ornamental. This is still a lead-driven feature, but the relationships are strong enough to keep the movie from feeling solitary.

lead_characters.name: Billy Butler
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 40s at start and 50s later, white, working-class, former MMA fighter, father
lead_characters.hook: Billy is a battered ex-cage fighter whose body is failing him, whose temper keeps dragging him back into violence, and whose love for his daughter is the only thing stronger than his self-destruction. He reads as a man who has spent years confusing survival with identity, and the script gives him a painful, playable arc from rage machine to present father. The role lives in the contradiction between tenderness at home and animal force in the ring.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Mickey Rourke in The Wrestler — a physically worn, emotionally exposed man whose body tells the story before he does. It gives an actor bruised charisma, fight choreography, grief, and a late-life redemption arc that can carry a movie.

lead_characters.name: Rollie
lead_characters.hook: Rollie is Billy’s old trainer and moral counterweight: blunt, loyal, and increasingly terrified of what Billy is doing to himself. He has the authority of a father figure without the sentimentality, and the script uses him as both conscience and tactical guide. He’s the kind of supporting role that can steal scenes with economy and lived-in disappointment.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Nick Nolte in Warrior or Burt Young in Rocky its bruised authority — a veteran with history, regret, and hard-earned wisdom. It offers a character actor a chance to play love as discipline and disappointment as devotion.

lead_characters.name: Jasmine
lead_characters.demographics: Female, late 30s, dark-skinned, pregnant partner and later deceased mother
lead_characters.hook: Jasmine is Billy’s emotional anchor and the script’s clearest voice of sanity: loving, practical, and unwilling to romanticize his violence. She’s not just the girlfriend; she’s the person who keeps naming the life Billy could choose instead. The role has warmth, steel, and real emotional consequence even after her death.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded, emotionally central supporting part that gave Regina King in If Beale Street Could Talk or Emily Blunt in A Quiet Place real gravity — love, fear, and moral clarity in a compressed space. It gives an actor intimate scenes, maternal stakes, and the chance to define the movie’s heart.

lead_characters.name: Cisco Montes
lead_characters.hook: Cisco is the smiling predator at the center of the machine: a promoter, fixer, and extortionist who speaks like a friend while operating like a mob boss. He’s the script’s most overtly dangerous presence because he understands Billy better than Billy understands himself. The role is all control, menace, and charm weaponized as business.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of sleek, threatening antagonist role that gave Javier Bardem in No Country for Old Men or Benicio del Toro in Sicario its cold electricity. It offers a performer the chance to be charismatic, terrifying, and always one step ahead.

lead_characters.name: Claudia
lead_characters.demographics: Female, child to teen over the course of the film, Billy’s daughter, medically fragile
lead_characters.hook: Claudia is the story’s emotional future: smart, funny, resilient, and forced to grow up around illness and fear. She gives the movie its innocence and its stakes, and the later time jumps let her become the living proof of what Billy fought for. She’s not passive; she pushes Billy toward better behavior and ultimately helps save him.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of child-to-young-teen role that gave Brooklynn Prince in The Florida Project or Abigail Breslin in Little Miss Sunshine its emotional authority. It gives a young actor humor, vulnerability, and the rare chance to be the moral center of an adult genre film.

lead_characters.name: Frank Stevens
lead_characters.hook: Frank is the hustler intermediary who turns Billy’s violence into cash, then into bigger trouble. He’s comic, greasy, and opportunistic, but the script also makes him useful enough to survive in the ecosystem. He functions as a pressure valve and a reminder that the fight world is built on grift as much as blood.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of fast-talking, morally compromised supporting role that gives a character actor room to riff, like Stephen Root in No Country for Old Men or Paul Walter Hauser in Richard Jewell. It’s a scene-stealing part with comic timing and real danger underneath.

lead_characters.name: Eduardo Cruz
lead_characters.demographics: Male, early 20s, Latino, elite fighter, Sergio’s son
lead_characters.hook: Eduardo is vengeance with a body: disciplined, lethal, and emotionally locked onto Billy as the man who ruined his family. He’s not just a final boss; he’s the living consequence of the opening fight, and that gives him a clean, mythic function. The role is built to be physically imposing and emotionally single-minded.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase lane of a young action lead like Michael B. Jordan in Creed or Taron Egerton in a physical prestige role — athletic dominance plus personal grievance. It gives an actor a chance to play a near-unstoppable opponent with real emotional charge.

lead_characters.name: Jimmy
lead_characters.hook: Jimmy is the comic, loyal friend who keeps Billy tethered to ordinary life while also getting pulled into the fight world. He’s funny without being a clown, and he gives the movie some oxygen between the bruises. The role is a classic best-friend support with enough personality to matter.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded buddy role that gave Michael Peña in End of Watch or Anthony Mackie in The Hurt Locker real texture — humor, loyalty, and emotional access without stealing the movie. It’s a strong supporting showcase for a likable, fast-talking actor.

lead_characters.name: Sarah
lead_characters.hook: Sarah is the practical adult in the room when Billy’s life is spinning out, and the script uses her to show how much labor Claudia’s care requires. She’s gentle, observant, and quietly emotionally exposed in the scene where she nearly kisses Billy. It’s a small but useful role that adds realism and pressure.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of intimate supporting part that gives an actor a clean, human scene opposite the lead, similar to the grounded caretakers in The Pursuit of Happyness or The Blind Side. It offers warmth, restraint, and a subtle emotional turn.

lead_characters.name: Dr. Bui
lead_characters.hook: Dr. Bui is the medical truth-teller who keeps forcing the story back to reality: Claudia is sick, Billy is disqualified as a donor, and time is running out. He’s not flashy, but he’s essential because he translates the stakes into hard facts. The role gives the film procedural credibility and emotional pressure.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded professional role that gives an actor authority and compassion in the mold of a medical or legal supporting part in a prestige drama. It’s a clean, credible scene partner role with real stakes.

casting_characteristics: One physically credible male lead in his 40s-50s who can sell fight wear and emotional exhaustion
One child performer who must play sick, resilient, and emotionally precise across a multi-year span
Supporting roles require believable fight-world texture and regional specificity

notable_requirements: Las Vegas strip and hotel interiors
Shreveport apartment, construction site, casino, and riverboat casino
Underground fight spaces including ballroom, swamp, barn, parking garage, alley, and riverbank
Hospital, operating room, and children’s hospital settings

technical.vfx_details: Primarily fight enhancement, blood, bruising continuity, and a few establishing aerials; no major digital worldbuilding.
technical.sfx_needs: Fight choreography, blood rigs, practical injury makeup, gunshot wound effects, rain, mud, and water-based fight staging.

rights_flags.detail: Mickey Rourke appears as himself in a cameo.
UFC is referenced in the opening Vegas establishing imagery.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Realistic release model is a theatrical or premium-streaming adult genre feature with strong male-skewing appeal and awards-adjacent performance potential.

budget.note: The script is contemporary and mostly practical, but the fight count, hospital material, rain/mud work, animal-adjacent swamp staging, and Vegas travel keep it above a simple contained indie.

casting.note: Billy needs a lead who can credibly play a damaged ex-fighter, a loving father, and a man in physical decline, while Claudia must carry a substantial emotional load across age jumps.

development.note: The central engine is clear, but the script’s emotional and commercial identity depends on balancing the fight-movie propulsion with the father-daughter medical drama and the Cisco/Crime angle.

comp_set.title: The Wrestler
comp_set.why_it_comps: A physically broken older combatant whose body is both his livelihood and his undoing, with a performance-first emotional spine.

comp_set.title: Warrior
comp_set.why_it_comps: Fight-world intensity fused to family trauma, with training, bouts, and redemption all tied to domestic stakes.

comp_set.title: Southpaw
comp_set.why_it_comps: A bruising boxing comeback story where grief, fatherhood, and punishment drive the action.

comp_set.title: Creed
comp_set.why_it_comps: The mentor/fighter legacy energy and the emotional logic of a combat story built around family and identity.

comp_set.title: The Florida Project
comp_set.why_it_comps: Not in genre, but in the child-centered emotional urgency and the way a kid’s perspective gives the adult world its stakes.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like bruising, emotional sports dramas with a clear underdog engine and a strong father-child hook.
audience_target.demographics: Skews male 25-54, but the parent-child stakes broaden it to women 30-54 who respond to emotional family drama; likely strongest with working- and middle-class audiences.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary locations, practical fight staging, and modest VFX keep it in indie feature territory, though the number of fight setups and hospital scenes require disciplined scheduling.

lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane where character pain, physical punishment, and emotional redemption are the selling points. The script has enough grit for genre buyers and enough heart for prestige-minded buyers looking for a lead performance vehicle.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature with a closed emotional arc; the supporting world is vivid, but there is no clear sequel or spinoff vector that would justify franchise framing.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The opening fight is a brutal thesis statement.
strengths.what_it_means: It tells a buyer immediately that the movie has a physical hook, a clear lead, and a visceral tone that can sell in a trailer. That makes the script easy to position for genre buyers and actors who want a showcase with impact.
strengths.evidence: Billy blacking out in the cage, winning by rage, and then not remembering the victory until after the bell.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The father-daughter engine is genuinely moving.
strengths.what_it_means: The Claudia material gives the movie emotional legitimacy beyond the fight scenes, which broadens the audience and makes the violence feel motivated rather than decorative. That is the kind of hook that attracts actors, producers, and buyers looking for a genre film with heart.
strengths.evidence: The pancakes, the dialysis routine, the chess scenes, and Billy’s repeated promise to keep Claudia alive.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Cisco is a strong, saleable antagonist.
strengths.what_it_means: A villain who is both criminal and intimate gives the movie a face and a pressure source that can carry marketing and performance conversations. Buyers like a clear human antagonist because it simplifies the pitch and sharpens the stakes.
strengths.evidence: Cisco paying doctors, threatening the family, and using Claudia as leverage to force Billy back into the cage.

strengths.what_it_means: The swamp fights, barn bouts, riverbank crowds, and crooked promotion ecosystem create a specific world that feels ownable and cinematic. That specificity helps the project stand out from generic boxing or MMA dramas.
strengths.evidence: Swamp Fights, the muddy riverbank cage, the barn ring, and the Vegas-to-Shreveport pipeline.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Billy is a strong late-career lead role.
strengths.what_it_means: The part offers a performer physical degradation, moral conflict, tenderness, and rage, which is exactly the kind of role that can reframe a mid-career or veteran actor. That is valuable packaging currency because it gives the project a clear casting conversation.
strengths.evidence: Billy’s body breaking down, his fear of head trauma, and his final choice to fight for Claudia rather than himself.

whats_special.headline: This is a bruising, emotionally legible father-daughter fight movie with a real performance role at the center and a vivid underworld around it. The combination of practical fight staging, a clear villain, and a contained contemporary footprint makes it a credible indie feature with streamer and boutique theatrical upside.

items.area: The ending leans hard on coincidence and escalation.
items.detail: Cisco’s organ-donor reveal, the cemetery confrontation, the kidnapping, the gunshot, and the final transplant resolution all stack very quickly in the last stretch. It’s a strong emotional payoff, but it also concentrates a lot of plot machinery into a narrow window, which is the main structural pressure point a buyer will notice.

items.area: Billy’s medical condition is a moving target.
items.detail: The script introduces a brain cyst, then later returns to the same head-trauma danger as the decisive obstacle, while Claudia’s kidney failure drives the emotional engine. That dual medical track gives the movie urgency, but it also creates a clarity issue around which condition is the true ticking clock at any given moment.

items.area: The fight repetition can feel episodic.
items.detail: Several middle sections follow the same pattern: Billy needs money, takes a fight, gets beaten, then wins by rage or grit. That repetition is useful for momentum, but it also means the movie’s middle third is highly dependent on the novelty of each fight setup and opponent.

items.area: Cisco’s leverage is almost too absolute.
items.detail: He owns the home, the medical access, the fight pipeline, and eventually the donor solution, which makes him an efficient villain but also a very dominant force in the story. That concentration of power is effective dramatically, though it narrows the range of plausible resistance around him.

items.area: The tone sits between prestige drama and exploitation.
items.detail: The script wants the emotional weight of a family drama while also delivering mud fights, cage violence, and a criminal underworld. That hybrid is a selling point, but it also means the project will need a buyer comfortable with both sentiment and brutality in the same package.

issues.headline: The main friction is structural, not conceptual: the movie has a strong hook, but the back half stacks medical, criminal, and revenge mechanics very aggressively. Buyers will respond to the lead role and the father-daughter stakes, then immediately ask how much of the final act is cleanly engineered versus heavily loaded.
